To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the yields of composites in the thermodynamic model are consistent with the droplet model parametrisation (ii) yields in a finite system can also be fitted by the same parametrisation (iii) the critical parameters deduced from this fitting are not reliable

(i) yields of nuclear disintegration can be calculated to high precision in a model with a first order phase transition; (ii) yields of nuclear fragments can be fitted with a formula derived in the context of the droplet model; (iii) yields can also be fitted with a parametrization derived from the mean field approximation of the liquid-gas critical point, but with parameters which have no obvious physical interpretation; (iv) yields can also fitted with a formula which is the usual form

(1) the model has a first order phase transition; (2) yields calculated in this finite model are not consistent with the usual critical power-law behaviour in the thermodynamic limits; (3) the best fit of yields to a power-law behaviour gives a value of $T_C$ that is very close to that at which the phase transition occurs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of yields of nuclear multifragmenation in a model where yields can be calculated to high accuracy.
the question of what can be learned from data on nuclear multifragmentation.

the question of whether one can extract critical exponents from the yields of nuclear disintegration and the answer is that one can do so only if one is very careful and if one uses the correct model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in this model, the critical temperature and exponents are not accessible from the yields of disintegration.
the yields in the model considered here are not consistent with the critical behaviour expected in a first order phase transition.

it is not possible to extract critical parameters, or indeed any information about the phase transition, from yields of disintegrating systems, even if one assumes that the system has a phase transition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, the model considered in this work does not have critical exponents which can be deduced from data on nuclear multifragmentation.
yields in nuclear disintegration are sensitive to the phase transition in the model, but it is not possible to extract critical parameters.
the model considered in the present work is a good model of multifragmentation, and the yields can be parametrised in terms of a single parameter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the thermodynamics limit, the model has first order phase transition.
the yields of composites are sensitive to the phase transition.
the critical parameters of a first order phase transition can be obtained only by a detailed analysis of the model.
